person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: method
span.quote: Through an in-depth analysis, the study identifies Named Graphs, RDF-star, the Provenance Ontology (PROV-O), Dublin Core (DC), Conjectural Graphs, and the OpenCitations Data Model (OCDM) as the most effective solutions.

span.label: provenance and change tracking for cultural heritage metadata in RDF
span.quote: However, tracking provenance and changes in metadata using the Resource Description Framework (RDF) presents significant challenges due to the limitations of foundational Semantic Web technologies.

span.label: systematic-review
span.quote: In order to conduct the review, we adopted a citation-based strategy (Figure 1), also known as “snowballing” (Wohlin, 2014), which consists of exploding the bibliography from a seed paper (Lecy & Beatty, 2012), which was Sikos & Philp (2020).

span.label: The TriG serialisation shown for RDF/S graphsets is the authors' own reconstruction, because no official serialisation exists.
span.quote: Please note that the TriG serialization presented here is a deduction based on the analysis of the master thesis works on RDF/S graphsets (Pediaditis, 2008) and its related paper (Pediaditis et al., 2009).

span.label: The RDF triple-coloring example is likewise a deduction rather than a published serialisation.
span.quote: The serialization provided in Listing 9 is therefore a deduction, based on the logical descriptions and algorithms found in Flouris et al. (2009).

span.label: No model surveyed has become a widely accepted standard for tracking both provenance and change.
span.quote: This limitation has led to the introduction of numerous metadata representation models, none of which have become widely accepted standards for tracking both provenance and changes in RDF entities.

span.label: Querying provenance recorded by the oldest W3C approach requires matching the whole original statement.
span.quote: Finally, composing SPARQL queries to obtain provenance annotated through RDF Reification is cumbersome: to identify the URI of the reification, it is necessary to explicitly match the entire reference triple

span.label: The alternative introduces a node that cannot be resolved from outside.
span.quote: However, a drawback of this approach is that the blank node introduced cannot be globally dereferenced, which can limit interoperability in certain contexts

span.label: The survey's verdict on which models are most effective is relative to three named criteria.
span.quote: These models are evaluated based on their compliance with RDF standards, scalability, and applicability across different domains

span.label: RDF Reification versus n-ary relations - SIMILAR IN STRUCTURE, DIFFERENT IN ONE NAMED RESPECT: reification turns the entire triple into an entity that can be annotated, while n-ary relations introduce an intermediary node that encodes the relationship, and the paper states this is a fundamental difference rather than a notational one
span.quote: From a structural perspective, n-ary relations share similarities with RDF Reification, but there is a fundamental difference in their approach. RDF Reification converts the entire triple into an entity that can be annotated with additional metadata, whereas n-ary relations introduce an intermediary node that encodes a reified relationship

span.label: a blank node - LOCALLY VALID, GLOBALLY UNRESOLVABLE: the node an n-ary relation introduces cannot be globally dereferenced, so the annotation exists inside one graph and cannot be pointed at from another, which is what the authors mean by limited interoperability
span.quote: However, a drawback of this approach is that the blank node introduced cannot be globally dereferenced, which can limit interoperability in certain contexts

span.label: most effective - EFFECTIVE ON THREE STATED CRITERIA: the survey's shortlist is chosen by compliance with RDF standards, scalability, and applicability across domains, so the word ranks the models on those axes and not on whether anyone adopted them - which the record's existing limitation says none did
span.quote: These models are evaluated based on their compliance with RDF standards, scalability, and applicability across different domains

span.label: builds-on → the classification framework of Sikos & Philp (2020)
span.quote: In our classification, we adopt the framework proposed by Sikos & Philp (2020), which categorizes these approaches based on multiple dimensions: semantics, tuple typology (i.e., the number of elements in an RDF tuple, such as triples, quadruples, or quintuples), standard compliance, reliance on external vocabularies, blank node management, granularity, and scalability.

span.label: builds-on → the provenance dimensions of the W3C Provenance Incubator Group (Gil et al., 2010)
span.quote: Provenance can be evaluated under three broad categories: content, management, and usage —as defined in the study by Gil et al. (2010).

span.label: contradicts → the W3C-recommended RDF Reification and n-ary relations approaches
span.quote: In summary, RDF Reification and n-ary relations are the only standard and alternative recommended by W3C to describe the provenance in RDF and have considerable design flaws.

span.label: n-ary relations —contrasted-with→ reification
span.quote: From a structural perspective, n-ary relations share similarities with RDF Reification, but there is a fundamental difference in their approach. RDF Reification converts the entire triple into an entity that can be annotated with additional metadata, whereas n-ary relations introduce an intermediary node that encodes a reified relationship

span.label: blank node —causes→ interoperability
span.quote: However, a drawback of this approach is that the blank node introduced cannot be globally dereferenced, which can limit interoperability in certain contexts

span.label: provenance information
span.quote: provenance information, i.e., contextual metadata, primarily related to the identification of entities

span.quote: a citation-based strategy (Figure 1), also known as “snowballing”
